1.title: Access, identity and user creation
1.scenario: You are the new support team. Establish individual identities before changing the shared loyalty server.
concepts: The SSH key authenticates a login; it does not make the login root.
A user, primary group, supplementary groups and home-directory permissions are separate controls.
Use sudo only for the supervised administrative step; keep routine investigation unprivileged.
steps: Create private evidence and confirm access
1.commands:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f "$HOME/.ssh/support_lab_ed25519"
cat "$HOME/.ssh/support_lab_ed25519.pub"

chmod 600 ~/pem/okada.pem
ssh -i ~/pem/okada.pem ubuntu@47.131.221.162
whoami
id
hostname
date -u +%FT%TZ

read -r -p 'Assigned learner name: ' learner
read -r -p 'Assigned team group: ' team
sudo adduser --disabled-password --gecos '' "$learner"
sudo groupadd -f "$team"
sudo usermod -aG "$team" "$learner"
sudo chmod 750 "/home/$learner"
sudo install -d -m 700 -o "$learner" -g "$learner" "/home/$learner/.ssh"

read -r -p 'Learner PUBLIC key (one line): ' learner_public_key
printf '%s\n' "$learner_public_key" | sudo tee "/home/$learner/.ssh/authorized_keys" >/dev/null
sudo chown "$learner:$learner" "/home/$learner/.ssh/authorized_keys"
sudo chmod 600 "/home/$learner/.ssh/authorized_keys"
sudo stat -c '%U %G %a %n' "/home/$learner/.ssh" "/home/$learner/.ssh/authorized_keys"

read -r -p 'Your assigned learner account: ' learner
ssh -i "$HOME/.ssh/support_lab_ed25519" "$learner@47.131.221.162"
whoami
id
printf 'HOME=%s\n' "$HOME"

mkdir -p ~/support-lab/evidence/m1-01
umask 077
printf 'private lab note\n' > ~/support-lab/private.txt
stat -c '%U %G %a %n' ~/support-lab/private.txt
id > ~/support-lab/evidence/m1-01/identity.txt
date -u +%FT%TZ >> ~/support-lab/evidence/m1-01/identity.txt

read -r -p 'A different learner account: ' other
sudo -u "$other" cat "/home/$learner/support-lab/private.txt"
checks: Learner logs in using their own key and has a writable home.
Private file has mode 600; team membership appears after a new login.
tricks: Does a # character inside a command prove you are root?
Why might id in an old shell omit a newly granted group?
Does chmod 777 fix a missing filesystem quota?
1.answer: Use id -u to establish identity. A new login refreshes supplementary groups. Directory traversal requires execute permission; read permission alone is insufficient. chmod changes access, not capacity. Keep ~/.ssh owned by its account and never place a private key in the course repository.
1.output: Identity baseline, permission evidence and a short access checklist.

1.title: Navigation, files and package installation
1.scenario: A deployment arrives as an archive. Find the right directory, inspect it, copy it safely and install diagnostic tools.
concepts: Absolute paths start at /; relative paths start at the current working directory.
Quote paths and distinguish copying a file from overwriting an existing destination.
apt is the Ubuntu package manager; dnf examples are Red Hat comparisons, not commands for this host.
steps: Create, copy and rename a file
Check the tools as a learner
Compress a copy and observe a broken link
1.commands:
mkdir -p ~/support-lab/files-practice/{incoming,work,archive}
cd ~/support-lab/files-practice
pwd
ls -lah
cd /var/log
pwd
cd -

printf 'alpha\nbeta\n' > 'incoming/status report.txt'
cp -i -- 'incoming/status report.txt' work/
mv -- 'work/status report.txt' work/status.txt
head -n 1 work/status.txt
ln -s status.txt work/latest
ls -l work
readlink work/latest

sudo apt-get update
apt-cache search '^lsof$'
sudo apt-get install -y curl netcat-openbsd dnsutils lsof sysstat
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/lsof

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
printf '%s\n' "$PATH"
command -v curl nc dig lsof pidstat
tar -tzf shared/fixtures/support-fixtures.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/support-lab/fixtures
tar -xzf shared/fixtures/support-fixtures.tar.gz -C ~/support-lab/fixtures

printf 'compress me\n' > ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/compression.txt
gzip -k ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/compression.txt
gzip -dc ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/compression.txt.gz
rm -i -- ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/status.txt
ls -l ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/latest
cat ~/support-lab/files-practice/work/latest
checks: Student explains why the symlink breaks after its target is removed.
Commands are found through PATH; package installation is verified rather than assumed.
tricks: Does cd /var/log change another terminal’s working directory?
Why is sudo echo text > /root/file different from echo text | sudo tee /root/file?
What happens when an unquoted variable contains spaces?
1.answer: The shell performs redirection before sudo runs echo. Use a deliberately approved destination and sudo tee when needed. cd changes the current process environment. A symlink stores a path and does not keep its target alive. Use -- before filenames when the tool supports it.
1.output: A directory tree, package verification table and safe file-handling notes.

1.title: Allocate space and diagnose disk limits
1.scenario: A learner reports “my EC2 user is capped.” Determine which layer is limiting writes before selecting a fix.
concepts: EBS volume → partition → filesystem → directory/account; growing one layer does not automatically grow all layers.
Compare byte capacity, inode capacity, quotas, permissions and deleted-open files.
The observed host already has an expanded root filesystem; reproduce growth on a disposable disk.
steps: Observe quota allocation; compare additional storage symptoms
1.commands:
id
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt -T "$HOME"
df -hT "$HOME"
df -i "$HOME"
quota -s

sudo repquota -a
sudo lsof +L1

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
less shared/scripts/storage-lab.sh
sudo shared/scripts/storage-lab.sh create
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo df -hT /var/lib/support-storage-lab/mount

sudo shared/scripts/storage-lab.sh grow
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo df -hT /var/lib/support-storage-lab/mount

sudo shared/scripts/storage-lab.sh cleanup
checks: Student identifies the limiting layer from evidence, not the wording of the complaint.
Disposable filesystem grows and can be cleaned up; root partition is untouched.
tricks: df says full but du is small: name three explanations.
Will adding a user allocate a new partition?
Why can root sometimes write when an ordinary user cannot, even without quotas?
1.answer: Possible causes include deleted-open files, hidden data under mounts, inaccessible paths during du, reserved ext4 blocks, inode exhaustion, quotas, or permissions. Normal user creation does not create a per-user EBS disk. Show inode and quota evidence before diagnosing a cap. EBS growth requires appropriate AWS access and a snapshot; grow the partition only if present, then the matching filesystem.
1.output: A storage decision tree and before/after capacity evidence.

1.title: Command investigations and first Bash script
1.scenario: Operations received mixed logs and filenames. Produce accurate incident counts without losing records or matching misleading text.
concepts: grep selects lines; awk interprets fields; sed transforms text; each has different quoting rules.
Sort before uniq, choose numeric sorting for numbers and preserve filenames with NUL separators.
Counts require a clear unit: lines, requests, users and incidents are not interchangeable.
Create and execute a small Bash evidence collector before the incident challenge.
steps: Inspect the evidence without editing it
Compare a naive search with parsed status
Observe an expected nonzero pipeline result
Inspect and execute your saved script
Change the input, then choose your own check
1.commands:
cd ~/support-lab/fixtures
less application.log
head -n 4 application.log
tail -n 4 application.log
wc -l application.log

grep -n ERROR application.log
grep -n 'status=5[0-9][0-9]' application.log
awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /^path=/) print $i}' application.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

tail -n +2 latency.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort -n
sed -n '2,6p' application.log
printf 'seen\n' | tee ~/support-lab/evidence/m1-04/pipeline.txt
date -u +%FT%TZ

find filenames -type f -print0 | xargs -0 -r wc -c
mkdir -p ~/support-lab/archive
find filenames -type f -print0 | tar --null -T - -czf ~/support-lab/archive/selected.tar.gz
verify_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/support-lab/archive/verify-XXXXXX")
tar -xzf ~/support-lab/archive/selected.tar.gz -C "$verify_dir"
diff -r filenames "$verify_dir/filenames"

previous_pipefail=$(set +o | grep pipefail)
set -o pipefail
grep 'NO_SUCH_REQUEST' application.log | wc -l
pipeline_rc=$?
printf 'pipeline_exit=%s\n' "$pipeline_rc"
eval "$previous_pipefail"

mkdir -p "$HOME/support-lab/bin"
if [[ -e "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh" ]]; then
    printf 'Keep existing triage.sh; inspect it before editing.\n'
else
    cat > "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh" <<'SCRIPT'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
service=${1:-support-tomcat}
printf 'UTC=%s service=%s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$service"
df -h "$HOME"
systemctl is-active "$service"
service_rc=$?
printf 'service_exit=%s\n' "$service_rc"
SCRIPT
fi
bash -n "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh" && chmod 750 "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh"
"$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh" > "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m1-04/first-script.txt"
cat "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m1-04/first-script.txt"

cat "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh"
if bash -n "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh"; then
    cd "$HOME"
    ./support-lab/bin/triage.sh support-tomcat
    printf 'collector_exit=%s\n' "$?"
fi
checks: Counts match parsed fixture records; malformed rows are reported separately.
All unusual filenames survive the archive round trip.
Run triage.sh with two service arguments and explain the captured statuses.
tricks: Does grep returning 1 always mean an error?
Will uniq find nonadjacent duplicates?
Can cut reliably parse arbitrary CSV with quoted commas?
1.answer: grep exits 1 for no matches, 2 for an error. uniq removes adjacent duplicates only. Basic cut is not a full CSV parser. A pipeline usually reports its last command status; pipefail changes this. Use NUL separators for arbitrary filenames. The fixture contains six valid requests, two 5xx errors, two slow requests at >=1000 ms, and one malformed row.
1.output: Pipelines, archive check and triage.sh with two-input test evidence.

1.title: Install and inspect the application stack

concepts: A Java runtime, servlet container, database and application configuration are separate dependencies.
systemd unit configuration defines process identity, environment, startup and restart behavior.
A live process is weaker evidence than an authenticated business request.
steps: Open a browser through SSH forwarding
1.commands:
cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
less shared/scripts/setup-ubuntu.sh
shared/scripts/preflight.sh

sudo shared/scripts/setup-ubuntu.sh --training-host
setup_rc=$?
printf 'setup_exit=%s\n' "$setup_rc"

practice_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/support-lab/unit-practice-XXXXXX")
cp "$COURSE_ROOT/shared/templates/service-practice.service" "$practice_dir/support-tomcat.service"
systemctl cat support-tomcat
nano "$practice_dir/support-tomcat.service"
cat "$practice_dir/support-tomcat.service"

systemctl cat support-tomcat
systemctl status support-tomcat --no-pager
journalctl -u support-tomcat --since '10 minutes ago' --utc --no-pager
ss -lnt

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/live
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/player?id=1'
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/report

read -r -p 'Assigned learner account: ' learner
ssh -N -L 18080:127.0.0.1:8080 -i "$HOME/.ssh/support_lab_ed25519" "$learner@47.131.221.162"
checks: Readiness returns 200 and player 1 returns synthetic data.
Student explains why Tomcat runs as supportapp and MySQL is not exposed publicly.
tricks: Does systemctl enable start a stopped service?
Can /live return 200 while the database password is wrong?
Why should you collect the journal before restart?

1.title: Service failures and application log diagnosis
1.scenario: The application worked before a change. One team investigates a startup fault; another receives a permission fault after reset.
concepts: Capture unit state, exit status and journal before changing configuration.
Correlate an HTTP response request ID with its application log line.
Distinguish startup failure, runtime failure and failed dependency checks.
steps: Introduce and observe a startup fault
Reset, then introduce a different failure
Inspect runtime symptoms and file access
1.commands:
date -u +%FT%TZ
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh startup

systemctl status support-tomcat --no-pager
systemctl cat support-tomcat
journalctl -u support-tomcat -n 60 --utc --no-pager

sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh reset
curl --fail -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health && sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh permissions

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health
journalctl -u support-tomcat --since '5 minutes ago' --utc --no-pager

sudo namei -l /etc/support-lab/app.properties
sudo stat -c '%U %G %a %n' /etc/support-lab/app.properties
sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh reset
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/player?id=1'
checks: Evidence names the actual failed executable or unreadable file.
Recovery includes HTTP and business checks, not only active service status.
tricks: Does a restart policy repair a bad executable path?
Does a missing ERROR line prove the service started?
Why is chmod 777 an inappropriate application-config fix?
1.answer: The startup drop-in overrides ExecStart; inspect both unit and drop-in. The permissions fault leaves root owning a mode-600 config, so supportapp cannot read it. Correct access is root:supportapp mode 640. Repeated restarts cannot fix either cause. Preserve the failure evidence before using reset.
1.output: A timeline with failing and recovered request IDs.

1.title: Resource and network troubleshooting
1.scenario: Users report intermittent errors. Determine whether CPU, memory, DNS, TCP, TLS or database authentication evidence supports the complaint.
concepts: High load is not the same measurement as CPU utilization; memory available differs from free.
A listening port and successful TCP connection do not prove database authentication.
Ubuntu firewall checks differ from Red Hat SELinux indicators; do not disable controls as a diagnostic shortcut.
steps: Observe bounded CPU and file handles
1.commands:
uptime
free -h
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,comm,pcpu,pmem --sort=-pcpu | head
top -b -n 1 | head -n 20
pidstat 1 3

timeout 15s bash -c 'while :; do :; done' &
worker_pid=$!
sudo lsof -p "$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value support-tomcat)" | head
wait "$worker_pid"
worker_rc=$?
printf 'worker_exit=%s\n' "$worker_rc"

getent hosts localhost
dig localhost
nslookup localhost
ping -c 2 127.0.0.1
traceroute -m 3 127.0.0.1
ss -lnt
nc -vz -w 2 127.0.0.1 3306
curl --max-time 5 -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health

sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh db-auth
nc -vz -w 2 127.0.0.1 3306
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health
sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh reset
checks: Student differentiates TCP reachability from successful authenticated queries.
Diagnosis cites interval evidence and acknowledges ICMP/filtering limitations.
tricks: Does failed ping prove the host is down?
Is low free memory alone proof of memory pressure?
Does curl -k repair an expired certificate?
1.answer: ICMP can be blocked while TCP works. Inspect available memory, swap/OOM evidence and workload behavior. curl -k bypasses validation and does not repair certificates. A MySQL listener can accept TCP while rejecting credentials. Red Hat AVC evidence requires policy/path investigation; do not teach disabling SELinux as the fix.
1.output: A layered connectivity table with evidence and remaining unknowns.

1.title: Linux incident challenge with your evidence script
1.scenario: A deployment left the loyalty application unavailable. Your team has 25 minutes to identify the fault and deliver a reusable evidence collector.
concepts: Build a small script from understood commands, then test failure behavior.
Record command failures without losing the rest of the incident evidence.
A recovery claim needs a customer-facing check and a clear incident summary.
steps: Receive the incident and assign roles
Propose one mitigation and define recovery
1.commands:
cp -i "$COURSE_ROOT/shared/templates/incident-report.md" "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m1-08/incident.md"
date -u +%FT%TZ
nano "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m1-08/incident.md"

nano "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh"

Incident report includes evidence, probable cause, mitigation and recovery validation.
tricks: Why can an evidence collector legitimately exit nonzero and still produce a useful bundle?
Does chmod +x guarantee a script will run on every shell?
1.answer: A partial bundle may contain a failed service-status check or a permission-denied log capture. Record those statuses instead of suppressing them. The interpreter in the shebang must exist; use Bash explicitly for Bash syntax. Grade reasoning and verified recovery above speed.

1.title: Advanced Linux command challenge bank
1.scenario: You must produce defensible answers from awkward input without changing source evidence.
concepts: Predict command behavior before running it.
Preserve evidence and explain assumptions about input format.
Robust pipelines handle empty input, malformed records and unusual filenames.
checks: Each answer includes an explanation and a counterexample where appropriate.
No command mutates original evidence or uses blanket deletion.
tricks: Is line count always record count?
When does tail -f miss a replacement log file?
Can grep ERROR count HTTP failures accurately?
1.answer: Use tail -F for following a filename across rotation when appropriate. wc -l counts newline characters. Parse explicit status fields rather than unstructured words. See instructor command-answer key for all 18 explanations.

2.title: Database baseline and safe access
2.scenario: The application reports database errors. Establish engine, endpoint, identity and connectivity before tuning anything.
concepts: Use a protected client option file instead of putting passwords in command arguments.
Read-only application rights differ from administrative diagnostic permissions.
Capture UTC time, engine version and connection counts with every baseline.
steps: Enter MySQL and identify the session
2.commands:
umask 077
touch "$HOME/.support-lab.cnf"
chmod 600 "$HOME/.support-lab.cnf"
nano "$HOME/.support-lab.cnf"

[client]
user=developer
password=password
host=localhost

stat -c '%a %n' "$HOME/.support-lab.cnf"
cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
MYSQL_CNF="$HOME/.support-lab.cnf" shared/scripts/db-health.sh
check_rc=$?
printf 'db_health_exit=%s\n' "$check_rc"

mysql --defaults-extra-file="$HOME/.support-lab.cnf"

SELECT UTC_TIMESTAMP(), CURRENT_USER(), VERSION();
SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_error';

systemctl status mysql --no-pager
journalctl -u mysql --since '15 minutes ago' --utc --no-pager
mysql --defaults-extra-file="$HOME/.support-lab.cnf" < shared/sql/mysql/diagnostics.sql
checks: Baseline identifies endpoint and effective database user.
Learner distinguishes access denied from server unreachable.
tricks: Can a successful SELECT 1 prove every business query is fast?
Does SHOW PROCESSLIST necessarily show all users to an unprivileged login?
2.answer: SELECT 1 checks a narrow path. PROCESS privilege controls visibility of other sessions; missing privileges can hide incident evidence. Do not distribute the application account password to learners. Use per-team diagnostic accounts and instructor-controlled writes.
2.output: A database baseline and a protected client configuration, never submitted with its password.

2.title: MySQL slow-query capture and ranking
2.scenario: Player reports are slow. Capture an intentional slow query and rank work by both frequency and total time.
concepts: Slow logging is a configuration change and must be restored after the exercise.
Global long_query_time becomes the default for new sessions; existing sessions may retain their value.
Frequency, total time, rows examined and lock time answer different questions.
steps: Inspect the capture and rank the fixture
checks: Slow record appears with query time, lock time and row counts.
Report explains why a frequent moderate query may cost more overall than one rare slow query.
tricks: Does Query_time alone prove CPU pressure?
Will changing a global threshold rewrite existing sessions?
2.answer: Elapsed time includes waiting and is not a CPU measurement. Use fresh sessions or an explicit session setting. Supplied evidence has a frequent player-report query and a rarer long query; compare total impact rather than selecting only the largest individual duration.
2.output: A ranked slow-query table with units, frequency and next checks.

2.title: EXPLAIN, indexes and misleading assumptions
2.scenario: The report scans many transactions. Decide whether a targeted index improves this workload.
concepts: EXPLAIN estimates access strategy and cardinality; it is not proof of actual elapsed time.
Indexes add write/storage costs and must be justified by workload.
A tiny training dataset may show plan differences without dramatic timing differences.
steps: Inspect data and the estimated plan
Compare after-state without assuming faster timing
checks: Before/after plans and equivalent query results are retained.
Recommendation includes an index tradeoff and measurement limitation.
tricks: Is every full scan bad?
Can an index be present yet unused?
Does LIMIT guarantee cheap execution?
2.answer: Full scans may be optimal for small tables or low-selectivity predicates. Expressions, types, selectivity and statistics affect index use. LIMIT can still require scanning or sorting many rows. For 100,000 seeded rows, player 42 has 1,000 transactions totaling 10,000.00.
2.output: A before/after plan comparison and an evidence-based recommendation.

2.title: MySQL blocking and deadlocks
2.scenario: Two concurrent updates stall. Separate an ordinary lock wait from a deadlock and recover both sessions.
concepts: A blocking chain can persist without a cycle; a deadlock requires a cycle.
The deadlock victim is not necessarily the root cause.
An open transaction can hold locks even while its client appears idle.
steps: Build the deadlock in a precise order
checks: Evidence shows the blocking relation or deadlock cycle.
Both sessions end their transactions and a subsequent update succeeds.
tricks: Does killing the waiting session remove the head blocker?
Does retrying immediately forever solve deadlocks safely?
2.answer: Killing a waiter does not release locks held by the blocker. Deadlock detection rolls back a victim; the survivor may still need an explicit rollback in this exercise. Retry only a complete safe transaction, with bounds/backoff and idempotency considerations.
2.output: A lock diagram, deadlock interpretation and verified cleanup.

2.title: Replication delay and reporting freshness
2.scenario: A reporting screen shows stale points while the primary accepts transactions. This is a supplied evidence exercise, not a configured replica.
concepts: Application routing and replica freshness must be investigated together.
Replication threads, errors and delay metrics need timestamps and context.
An empty replica-status result on a standalone server is not a replication failure.
steps: Read the fixture and record provenance
checks: Student recognizes NULL delay as unknown rather than healthy.
Recommendation addresses stale reads and the replication error separately.
tricks: Does a running receiver thread prove the applier is current?
Can reporting freshness be inferred from one lag number alone?
2.answer: The synthetic replica receiver is running but SQL applier stopped with duplicate-key error 1062. NULL lag is not zero. Investigate consistency and cause before repair; temporary primary reads require capacity and business approval.
2.output: A replication escalation note with evidence and routing tradeoffs.

2.title: SQL Server requests, sessions and wait deltas
2.scenario: SQL Server is blamed for high CPU. Capture active work and distinguish current activity from cumulative counters.
concepts: SQL Server 2022 diagnostic permissions differ from older examples; validate visibility first.
Requests and sessions are related but not interchangeable.
Wait statistics are cumulative; compare two captures over a known interval.
steps: Set connection details in the client shell
2.commands:
read -r -p 'SQL Server hostname or private IP: ' SQL_HOST
read -r -p 'Assigned SQL login: ' SQL_LOGIN
read -r -s -p 'SQL password: ' SQLCMDPASSWORD
printf '\n'
export SQL_HOST SQL_LOGIN SQLCMDPASSWORD
SQL_TLS_ARGS=()
command -v sqlcmd

sqlcmd "${SQL_TLS_ARGS[@]}" -S "tcp:$SQL_HOST,1433" -U "$SQL_LOGIN" -d SupportLab -b -Q 'SELECT SYSUTCDATETIME(), SUSER_SNAME(), @@VERSION;'

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
sqlcmd "${SQL_TLS_ARGS[@]}" -S "tcp:$SQL_HOST,1433" -U "$SQL_LOGIN" -d SupportLab -b -i shared/sql/sqlserver/diagnostics.sql -o "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m2-06/sql-baseline.txt"
less "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m2-06/sql-baseline.txt"

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
sqlcmd "${SQL_TLS_ARGS[@]}" -S "tcp:$SQL_HOST,1433" -U "$SQL_LOGIN" -d SupportLab -b -i shared/sql/sqlserver/workload.sql

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
cat shared/fixtures/sqlserver-waits.csv
checks: Report includes time window, permissions and correct units.
Student separates historical high waits from interval changes.
tricks: Can a sleeping session be the head blocker?
Does highest total_worker_time identify the currently slowest query?
2.answer: A sleeping session may hold an uncommitted transaction. Cached totals aggregate executions since compilation and do not necessarily describe this incident. Inspect execution_count, interval evidence and plans together. In the fixture LCK_M_X grows 12,000 ms, SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD 1,000 ms, and PAGEIOLATCH_SH 200 ms.
2.output: A SQL Server baseline and a wait-delta interpretation.

2.title: Blocking chains, Query Store and job failures
2.scenario: A deployment coincides with latency and a failed reporting job. Establish whether the symptoms share a cause.
concepts: Identify the head blocker through sessions as well as active requests.
Query Store compares plans and runtime intervals; correlation with deployment is not proof of causation.
SQL Agent job outcome and step outcome need separate interpretation.
steps: Create a bounded wait in B
Live extension — Compare a controlled index change
Live extension — Start the intentional job failure
Live extension — Read job history with the learner login
Compare captured Query Store and job evidence
checks: Capture a blocking relation and roll back both sessions.
Compare Query Store duration/reads and identify the failed job step using live or explicitly synthetic evidence.
tricks: Does a changed plan guarantee a regression?
Is plan forcing always the safest first action?
Can a failed job explain stale reports without explaining API latency?
2.answer: Compare runtime evidence across comparable intervals and row counts. Plan forcing needs validation and rollback. The fixture shows query 17 changing from plan 3 to 8 with higher duration/reads after deployment, while the job failure is a separate permission issue. The live training job deliberately throws a synthetic error.
2.output: A blocking worksheet, plan comparison and job-failure escalation.

2.title: Application/database correlation
2.scenario: An HTTP request took five seconds, but its database query took 40 milliseconds. Determine where the rest of the time went.
concepts: Application latency includes pool waits, SQL time, retries and downstream work.
Correlate IDs and UTC windows; acknowledge clock skew and missing instrumentation.
Request IDs in app logs do not automatically appear in database logs.
steps: Read and reconcile the synthetic request timing
2.commands:
cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
cat shared/fixtures/correlation.csv

shared/scripts/traffic.sh http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty 5

checks: Timeline accounts for measured time without inventing an exact database-request-ID join.
Learner distinguishes the sample app’s behavior from the supplied pooled-app evidence.
tricks: Does slow HTTP prove slow SQL?
Can retries amplify a partial outage?
2.answer: The supplied request waits 4,000 ms for a pool connection, spends 40 ms in SQL and 960 ms elsewhere. The live latency fault intentionally delays after connecting; it is not a real pool implementation. Repeated retries can increase load and duplicate non-idempotent work.
2.output: A correlated timeline and a targeted escalation request.

2.title: Final database incident challenge
2.scenario: A reporting request regressed after a release while ordinary player lookup remains responsive. Distinguish competing database causes using a separate synthetic incident pack.
concepts: Quantify changes in workload, query cost and result equivalence.
Test competing causes with discriminating evidence.
Define a reversible correction and bounded database-health checks.

Propose one mitigation and define recovery

3.title: Extend your Bash script into a health check
3.scenario: Turn yesterday’s commands into a script another engineer can run reliably.
concepts: Quote expansions; treat arguments as data; use arrays for command arguments.
Exit codes are an interface: document healthy, unhealthy and usage outcomes.
set -e is not a substitute for deliberate error handling.
steps: Create a script you can edit
Test an expected failure without changing services
Test your own validation and array behavior
3.commands:
mkdir -p ~/support-lab/bin
cat "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh"
if [[ ! -e "$HOME/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh" ]]; then
    cp "$HOME/support-lab/bin/triage.sh" "$HOME/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh"
fi
nano "$HOME/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
if (( $# > 2 )); then
    printf 'Usage: %s [service [http(s)-url]]\n' "$0" >&2
    exit 2
fi
service=${1-support-tomcat}
url=${2-http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health}
if [[ -z "$service" || "$service" == -* || "$service" == *[[:space:]]* ]]; then
    printf 'Invalid service\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
case "$url" in
    http://?*|https://?*) ;;
    *) printf 'Invalid URL\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
failed=0
log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$1"; }
for tool in systemctl curl timeout date; do
    command -v "$tool" >/dev/null || exit 2
done
probe_args=(--fail --silent --show-error --max-time 5)
if timeout 5 systemctl is-active --quiet "$service"; then
    log 'service=OK'
else
    log 'service=FAIL'; failed=1
fi
if curl "${probe_args[@]}" "$url" >/dev/null; then
    log 'endpoint=OK'
else
    log 'endpoint=FAIL'; failed=1
fi
exit "$failed"

bash -n ~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh
chmod 750 ~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh
~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh
script_rc=$?
printf 'script_exit=%s\n' "$script_rc"

~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh support-tomcat http://127.0.0.1:1
script_rc=$?
printf 'script_exit=%s\n' "$script_rc"

~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh support-tomcat http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health extra
printf 'extra_argument_exit=%s\n' "$?"
~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh support-tomcat file:///etc/passwd
printf 'invalid_url_exit=%s\n' "$?"
~/support-lab/bin/my-health.sh '' http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/health
printf 'empty_service_exit=%s\n' "$?"

less "$COURSE_ROOT/shared/scripts/health-check.sh"
DISK_LIMIT=invalid "$COURSE_ROOT/shared/scripts/health-check.sh"
reference_rc=$?
printf 'reference_exit=%s\n' "$reference_rc"
checks: Your script returns 0 for healthy checks, 1 for an unreachable endpoint and 2 for invalid arguments or missing tools.
Explain the quoted option array; submit actual results from your own script.
tricks: What happens to $? after echo runs?
Why can set -e behave differently inside conditionals?
3.answer: Capture the status immediately after the command. Explicit if command; then branches make expected failures clear. The reference health checker validates the disk threshold and reports each check instead of stopping at the first unhealthy service.
3.output: A documented executable Bash health checker and test transcript.

3.title: Automated evidence collection
3.scenario: An escalation needs a portable evidence bundle even when some commands fail or lack permission.
concepts: Use restrictive permissions, unique timestamped directories and a manifest.
Capture stdout, stderr and exit status for each check.
Redaction needs review; a regex cannot guarantee removal of every secret.
steps: Inspect and exercise masking with synthetic input
3.commands:
cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
shared/scripts/collect-evidence.sh "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m3-02/bundles" '20 minutes ago'
collector_rc=$?
printf 'collector_exit=%s\n' "$collector_rc"

read -r -p 'Printed archive path: ' bundle
stat -c '%a %n' "$bundle"
tar -tzf "$bundle"
review_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m3-02/review-XXXXXX")
tar -xzf "$bundle" -C "$review_dir"
find "$review_dir" -name manifest.tsv -exec cat {} \;

printf 'password=synthetic-only token=dummy-token\n' | sed -E 's/((password|token|secret|authorization)[=:][[:space:]]*)[^[:space:]]+/\1[REDACTED]/Ig'
checks: Failed checks remain visible in the manifest.
Bundle contains no credentials or environment dumps and is reviewed before sharing.
tricks: Can a timestamp alone prevent simultaneous filename collisions?
Should permission denied be silently converted to an empty success file?
3.answer: mktemp adds uniqueness; umask 077 restricts access. Nonzero capture results set partial=1 while preserving the rest of the bundle. Do not collect unrestricted environment/process argument data. Structured sensitive values may need stronger, format-aware redaction.
3.output: A reviewed evidence archive, manifest and evidence index.

3.title: Log parsing and threshold monitoring
3.scenario: Build a monitor that counts actual requests, rejects malformed rows and reports slow requests.
concepts: Define the time window, denominator, threshold comparison and no-data behavior.
Count status fields rather than words such as ERROR in free text.
A monitoring result is only as useful as its handling of missing or stale input.
steps: Compare healthy, empty and malformed cases

cd "$COURSE_ROOT"
shared/scripts/monitor-log.sh shared/fixtures/application.log 10 1000
monitor_rc=$?
printf 'monitor_exit=%s\n' "$monitor_rc"

for case_name in healthy empty malformed; do
    "$COURSE_ROOT/shared/scripts/monitor-log.sh" "$HOME/support-lab/evidence/m3-03/$case_name.log" 10 1000
    monitor_rc=$?
    printf '%s exit=%s\n' "$case_name" "$monitor_rc"
done

date -u +%FT%TZ > ~/support-lab/evidence/m3-03/captured-at.txt
journalctl -u support-tomcat --since '5 minutes ago' --utc -o cat --no-pager > ~/support-lab/evidence/m3-03/window.log
"$COURSE_ROOT/shared/scripts/monitor-log.sh" ~/support-lab/evidence/m3-03/window.log 10 1000

Empty input yields NO_DATA and exit 2, never healthy.
tricks: Is zero observed errors equivalent to a healthy service when no requests exist?
Should 404 responses count as server failures in this policy?
3.answer: The supplied policy counts status >=500 as server failures and latency >= threshold as slow. A rate equal to the threshold alerts. NO_DATA is unknown, not green. HTTP 4xx monitoring may be added separately according to business context.
3.output: A monitoring CSV and a written policy with denominator and no-data semantics.

Wrapper does not discard useful ALERT output because its exit code is 1.

Can identical timestamps prove causal linkage?

3.scenario: Your script works in a terminal but fails under cron. Make paths, permissions, concurrency and output explicit.
concepts: Cron supplies a smaller environment and different working directory.
Use absolute paths, a controlled PATH and a lock to prevent overlapping runs.
Cleanup is dry-run first, narrowly scoped and separate from incident evidence collection.

Back up and edit your own crontab
Verify the saved entry and observe execution
Preview, apply and verify narrowly scoped cleanup

Why can overlapping checks create a monitoring problem?

3.title: Deployment verification and maintenance boundaries
3.scenario: A deployment health gate must catch a business failure even if the process is active.

3.commands:

curl --fail --silent --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/payment

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
if ! body=$(curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 5 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/loyalty/player?id=1'); then
    printf 'player=UNREACHABLE\n'; exit 1
fi
if [[ $body != '1,Synthetic Player One,100' ]]; then
    printf 'player=UNEXPECTED_RESULT\n'; exit 1
fi
printf 'player=OK\n'
# Add a bounded payment check here; return nonzero if it fails.
exit 0

bash -n ~/support-lab/bin/deployment-check.sh
chmod 750 ~/support-lab/bin/deployment-check.sh
~/support-lab/bin/deployment-check.sh
gate_rc=$?
printf 'gate_exit=%s\n' "$gate_rc"

sudo shared/scripts/fault.sh reset
checks: Gate fails on affected business functionality even when Tomcat remains active.
Recovery checks cover the same function that originally failed.
tricks: Can a generic /health route detect every business outage?
Should the first failed probe trigger a database restart?
